lessonTitle: Wellbeing, Fatigue and Burnout: Recognising Risk, Finding Support and Protecting Your Health

blocks.text: It is 08:40 after your fourth night shift in a row. Driving home, you realise you have no memory of the last two junctions, and the car drifted across the line before you jerked awake. You are not careless; you are impaired by sleep loss in exactly the way you would warn a patient about. Looking after yourself is not a luxury in medicine, it is part of keeping patients safe.

blocks.markdown: Doctors work long hours, face emotionally demanding situations and carry responsibility, and so they are at risk of **fatigue**, **stress**, **burnout** and mental illness. The risks are highest in the first years of work, when responsibility is new and rotas are demanding. This unit covers how to recognise the effects of fatigue and burnout on your performance, where to find support and when to use it, and what the General Medical Council expects of doctors with regard to their own health. Policies and services vary between trusts and nations, so check what is available locally.

blocks.title: Burnout
blocks.text: In the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition, resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It has three dimensions: feelings of energy depletion or exhaustion, increased mental distance from the job or feelings of negativism or cynicism, and reduced professional efficacy.

rows: Pressure that feels manageable with resources
Illness with biological and psychological factors
Sleepiness, slower reactions, lapses of attention
Exhaustion, cynicism, reduced sense of achievement
Persistent low mood or loss of interest, poor sleep and appetite, worthlessness, possible thoughts of self-harm
Address workload and meaning at work, seek support
Medical assessment by a GP or appropriate service
Cynicism, withdrawal or errors are increasing
Any thoughts of self-harm or suicide
blocks.caption: Fatigue, stress, burnout and depression overlap but are not the same; this table is a teaching guide, not a diagnostic tool.

blocks.markdown: **Effects of fatigue.** Sleep loss and working at the circadian low point (usually in the small hours) reduce attention, memory, reaction time, decision-making and mood, and increase the risk of errors, needle-stick injuries and road traffic accidents on the drive home. Importantly, tired people are poor at judging how impaired they are. Prolonged wakefulness has been compared in studies to the effects of alcohol on performance, so the principle for patient safety is the same: do not assume you are performing as normal after a night with no sleep. Working time rules, rest requirements and exception reporting arrangements exist to protect doctors and patients; check the details of the regulations and your contract.

blocks.title: How long have I been awake?
blocks.prompt: A foundation doctor woke at 07:00 on Monday, worked a normal day, slept briefly for about 20 minutes and then worked a night shift from 21:00 on Monday to 09:00 on Tuesday. Estimate how long she has been awake at 09:00 on Tuesday and decide what she should do about getting home.

steps.text: Count the time between waking and the end of the shift: from 07:00 Monday to 07:00 Tuesday is 24 hours, then a further 2 hours to 09:00 Tuesday, giving 26 hours.
Adjust for the short nap: a 20-minute nap helps slightly with alertness but does not reset the clock, so she is still effectively close to 26 hours of sustained wakefulness.

Recognise the risk: after this long awake, attention and reaction times are markedly impaired, the risk of falling asleep at the wheel is high, and her own judgement of how alert she feels is unreliable.
Choose a safer plan: arrange a lift, taxi or public transport, or sleep at the hospital in a rest facility before driving, and tell the team if the rota is repeatedly leaving no safe way home.
Plan the follow-up: report persistent fatigue, use exception reporting if hours exceed the agreed pattern, and review your sleep routine and rota with your supervisor.

blocks.answer: About 26 hours awake; she should not drive home drowsy. Use alternative transport or sleep first, and raise the rota problem through the appropriate route.

items: Take breaks, drink water and eat regular, balanced meals during long shifts.
Use rest facilities and short planned naps where policy allows; avoid caffeine late in a shift if you need to sleep afterwards.
Do not drive home drowsy: nap first, use a lift or taxi, or use public transport.
Protect sleep after nights: darkness, quiet and a regular routine.
Tell a colleague, nurse in charge or supervisor if you are too tired to practise safely.

blocks.markdown: **Seeking support.** Support is available at several levels. Informally, colleagues, friends and family can listen. Formally, your educational and clinical supervisors, the foundation programme director and your trust's wellbeing and occupational health services provide advice, workplace adjustments and referral. Your own GP provides confidential medical care. Doctors and dentists in England can use the NHS Practitioner Health service, and professional bodies and charities provide helplines; check which services are current and available where you work. In a crisis, including thoughts of harming yourself, seek urgent help immediately: contact emergency services, an emergency department or a crisis line such as Samaritans on 116 123 (UK) or your NHS urgent mental health service.

rows: Early stress or a bad day
Guidance on workload, rota, performance and wellbeing, and links to other services
Persistent difficulty, concerns about performance, or adjustments needed
Assessment of fitness for work, workplace adjustments
A health condition affecting work or the need for adjustments
Symptoms lasting more than a couple of weeks, sleep or mood problems, any health concern
Confidential support for doctors, for example NHS Practitioner Health in England
Mental health or addiction concerns, or when you want a doctor-focused service
Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, or risk to yourself or others
blocks.caption: Sources of support and when to use them; confirm local availability.

blocks.markdown: **Professional responsibility for your own health.** The General Medical Council's Good medical practice expects doctors to take reasonable steps to protect their own health, be registered with a GP, and not diagnose or treat themselves or those close to them. If you have a health condition that could affect patients, you should seek medical advice and follow it, and, where appropriate, tell your employer or occupational health and take steps to protect patients, including adjusting your practice; you must not rely on your own assessment of the risk to patients. Seeking help is consistent with professional responsibilities and does not by itself threaten registration; check the current guidance and ask your medical defence organisation or the GMC if you are unsure. Doctors also have a duty to support colleagues who are struggling and to raise concerns if patients may be at risk.

blocks.title: Spotting burnout and making a plan
blocks.prompt: In the sixth month of work, a foundation doctor notices that she is exhausted even after days off, has started to feel that patients are 'just another task', and thinks that nothing she does makes a difference. She has made two small prescribing errors this month. Identify the burnout dimensions and outline a plan.

steps.text: Map each feature onto the dimensions: exhaustion even after rest matches energy depletion; treating patients as 'just another task' matches cynicism or mental distance; thinking nothing she does matters matches reduced efficacy.
Note the safety signal: two prescribing errors suggest that her state is affecting performance and patients, which makes timely action a professional duty as well as a wellbeing issue.

Rule out other contributors: ask about low mood, sleep, anxiety, alcohol use and any thoughts of self-harm; if persistent low mood or these thoughts are present she should see her GP or an urgent service promptly.
Take practical steps: speak to her educational supervisor about workload and rota, use occupational health for support, protect rest days, and use peer support or a reflective group.
Set review points: agree a plan with dates, report the errors through the incident system as a learning event, and re-evaluate in a few weeks, seeking further help earlier if she feels worse.

blocks.answer: She shows all three dimensions of burnout with an effect on safety; she should seek support from supervisor, occupational health and GP, explore for depression, report the errors and review the plan.

blocks.title: Do not wait for a crisis
blocks.text: Persistent exhaustion, cynicism, errors, increased alcohol use or any thoughts of self-harm are signals to act now. Many doctors delay seeking help because of fear of stigma or of consequences for their career; however, early help is better for you and for patients, and confidential services exist for exactly this reason.

points: Fatigue impairs attention, memory and decision-making and you cannot reliably judge your own impairment; do not drive home drowsy.
Burnout has three dimensions (exhaustion, cynicism or distance, reduced efficacy) and is different from depression, which needs medical assessment.
Support runs from colleagues and supervisors to occupational health, your GP and doctor-specific services; seek urgent help for thoughts of self-harm.
Professional duty includes protecting your own health, being registered with a GP, not self-treating and acting on advice if your health could affect patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly lists the three dimensions of burnout described in ICD-11?

options.text: Anxiety, insomnia and weight loss
Exhaustion, increased mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy
Low mood, loss of interest and suicidal thoughts
Overwork, poor pay and long commutes

questions.correctOptionText: Exhaustion, increased mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy

distractorRationale.a: These can accompany stress but are not the defining dimensions.
distractorRationale.c: These describe depression, a different problem.
distractorRationale.d: These are possible causes, not dimensions.

questions.explanation: Burnout is defined by exhaustion, cynicism or detachment from work and a sense of reduced effectiveness. Low mood and suicidal thoughts point to depression, which needs medical assessment even if the two overlap.

questions.stem: A doctor has been awake for 24 hours after a long on-call. Which effect is most likely?

options.text: Slower reaction times, reduced attention and poorer decision-making, with limited awareness of the impairment
Better memory for new instructions
No change in performance if the doctor feels alert
Improved concentration through adrenaline

questions.correctOptionText: Slower reaction times, reduced attention and poorer decision-making, with limited awareness of the impairment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fatigue impairs performance and insight.
distractorRationale.b: Memory and learning are impaired by sleep loss.
distractorRationale.d: Not a reliable effect; performance falls.

questions.explanation: Prolonged wakefulness reduces vigilance and judgement, and fatigued people tend to underestimate how impaired they are. This is why rest, breaks and safe travel home matter for patients and doctors alike.

questions.stem: A second-year foundation doctor has become sarcastic about patients, calling them 'bed numbers', has stopped attending teaching and dreads each shift. He says he is sleeping reasonably, his mood outside work is fine and he has no thoughts of self-harm. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take sedative medicines from a friend to cope
Ignore the feelings because everyone finds the training years hard
Work extra shifts to prove that he is coping
Speak to his educational supervisor and consider occupational health or his GP, recognising these features as signs of burnout

questions.correctOptionText: Speak to his educational supervisor and consider occupational health or his GP, recognising these features as signs of burnout

distractorRationale.a: Self-treatment is unsafe and against professional guidance.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: early help and workplace review.

questions.explanation: Cynicism, detachment and dread of work fit burnout, and the right response is to seek support early through supervisors and health services. Self-treatment and working harder worsen both safety and wellbeing.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor has had low mood and poor sleep for more than a month and wants confidential medical advice. Which source of support is most appropriate?

options.text: Waiting for the end of the rotation
Treating herself with medicines from the ward
Her own GP, or a doctor-specific service such as NHS Practitioner Health where available
Asking a colleague to prescribe for her informally

questions.correctOptionText: Her own GP, or a doctor-specific service such as NHS Practitioner Health where available

distractorRationale.d: Informal prescribing for colleagues is inappropriate.

questions.explanation: A GP provides confidential assessment and treatment, and doctor-specific services give additional support, so these are the right routes for persistent symptoms. Self-medication or informal prescribing breaches professional standards and risks harm.

questions.stem: Good medical practice from the General Medical Council expects doctors to be registered with a GP and not to diagnose or treat themselves.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Doctors are expected to take reasonable steps to protect their own health, and independent medical care avoids the blind spots of self-assessment and self-treatment. Check the current version of the guidance for exact wording.

questions.stem: You notice that a fellow foundation doctor has been tearful on several occasions, is arriving late and has made two prescribing errors this week. She tells you she is 'fine'. Discuss how you would approach this and what factors you would take into account.
markingGuide: Choose a private, supportive moment and express concern about specific observations without judgement
Listen, acknowledge distress, avoid diagnosing and encourage her to seek help, for example from her GP, supervisor or a doctor-specific service
Explain that support is available and that seeking help is consistent with professional duty
Recognise the limits of confidentiality: if patients may be at risk, you must tell a senior or supervisor
Consider the prescribing errors as a safety issue to be reported through the incident system, supportively
Offer to help in practical ways, and follow up later
Look after your own wellbeing and do not carry the burden alone
questions.explanation: The strongest answers combine compassion with professional duty: encourage help-seeking, protect patients and accept that confidentiality has limits. Credit goes for avoiding diagnosis and for naming specific, concrete supports.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor has been diagnosed with a condition that could, at times, affect her ability to practise safely. Which approach best fits professional responsibility?

options.text: Rely on her own judgement that she is safe to work
Keep the diagnosis secret to avoid career consequences
Stop all medical care and manage the condition alone
Seek medical advice, follow it, and involve occupational health or her employer as appropriate so that adjustments protect patients

questions.correctOptionText: Seek medical advice, follow it, and involve occupational health or her employer as appropriate so that adjustments protect patients

distractorRationale.b: Withholding it can leave patients at risk.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: adheres to duties to patients and self.

questions.explanation: Doctors must protect patients from risk that their own health might cause, and this means obtaining independent advice, following it and, where appropriate, telling the employer or occupational health. Concealment or reliance on one's own judgement is incompatible with this duty.

questions.stem: After a night shift you feel very sleepy at 09:00 and have a 40-minute drive home. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Drink several coffees and then drive
Drive carefully and stop only if you start to feel very tired
Do not drive while drowsy; sleep first in a rest facility or arrange a lift, taxi or public transport
Drive with the windows open and the radio loud

questions.correctOptionText: Do not drive while drowsy; sleep first in a rest facility or arrange a lift, taxi or public transport

distractorRationale.a: Caffeine gives only limited, temporary benefit.
distractorRationale.d: These measures do not reliably prevent sleep-related crashes.

questions.explanation: Drowsy driving causes crashes and a doctor has a responsibility to avoid unsafe situations. Safe alternatives include sleeping before the journey or using someone else's driving, and the rota issue should be raised.

questions.stem: You start your first rotation in two weeks. Outline a personal plan to protect your wellbeing, name the sources of support available to you and describe the signs that would make you seek help.
markingGuide: Registers with a GP and avoids self-treatment
Plans sleep, meals, exercise, social contact and breaks, and uses rest facilities during shifts
Identifies supports: peers, educational supervisor, occupational health, GP and doctor-specific services
Knows how to reach urgent help (emergency services, crisis lines such as Samaritans on 116 123)
Lists warning signs: persistent exhaustion, cynicism, low mood, errors, increased alcohol use, withdrawal or thoughts of self-harm
Commits to seeking help early and to raising rota or safety problems through exception reporting or the supervisor
Recognises responsibility to protect patients if health affects practice
questions.explanation: A good plan is specific, includes professional duties such as registering with a GP, and lists both supports and warning signs. Seeking help early is part of professional responsibility, not a sign of weakness.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor has had persistent low mood, loss of pleasure in everything, poor sleep, a sense of worthlessness and occasional thoughts that others would be better off without her for three weeks. She says 'it is just burnout'. What is the best interpretation and action?

options.text: These features suggest possible depression with risk, so she needs prompt medical assessment, for example by her GP or an urgent service
Fatigue only, so she should work fewer night shifts
A normal response to training that needs no help
Burnout only, so a few days off will fix it

questions.correctOptionText: These features suggest possible depression with risk, so she needs prompt medical assessment, for example by her GP or an urgent service

distractorRationale.a: Correct: persistent pervasive low mood with thoughts of self-harm needs urgent assessment.
distractorRationale.b: Rota changes may help but do not address the risk.
distractorRationale.d: Underestimates a possible depressive illness and risk.

questions.explanation: Pervasive low mood, loss of pleasure, worthlessness and thoughts of self-harm are features of depression rather than burnout alone, and the presence of thoughts of self-harm makes the situation urgent. Prompt assessment by a GP or crisis service is needed and her supervisors can help with time off.
